query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short, controlled pre-oxidation step (e.g. 10–30 min at ~700 °C in air) on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will grow a stable chromium-rich oxide layer that substantially reduces friction and wear as compared to the untreated alloy when sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized (as-cast or solution-annealed) CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with no prior surface treatments.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidizing environment at ~700 °C for 10–30 minutes to create a thin, adherent Cr-rich oxide scale on the surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests under a normal load around 10 N in ambient air, at temperatures incrementally increased from ~25 °C to ~800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable, chromium-rich oxide tribofilm on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Once formed, the oxide film prevents direct metal–metal contact, suppresses surface adhesion, and mitigates oxidative wear, enabling a self-lubricating effect across the temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy will exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient (e.g., ~0.2–0.3) and reduced wear rate compared to untreated CoCrFeNi across 25–800 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi tested under the same load and environment typically shows a friction coefficient exceeding ~0.4–0.6 and a higher wear rate, especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Sufficient chromium content to form stable surface oxides is needed. Performance is validated for loads near 10 N and temperatures up to 800 °C in air; other environments or operating conditions remain unverified.
generation.uncertainty: It is unclear how prolonged high-temperature exposure or contaminants may affect oxide integrity, and whether the approach remains robust at higher loads or beyond 800 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct sliding tests on (1) pre-oxidized and (2) non-pre-oxidized CoCrFeNi samples from 25 °C to 800 °C. After measuring friction and wear, remove the oxide layer from the pre-oxidized samples (e.g., with mechanical polishing) and retest to compare performance.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across all temperatures
Wear rates from volumetric loss analysis of the wear track at each test temperature
Surface characterization of oxide scale integrity before and after friction testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If friction and wear performance remain improved even after the oxide film is removed or no significant difference is observed between pre-oxidized and untreated samples, the hypothesis is invalidated.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC5706259, 2017) on near-Cantor CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys tested oxide dispersion strengthening (adding Y2O3) for room-temperature wear resistance but did not address high-temperature friction stability. Later efforts (PMC7311485, 2020) revealed that refining the near-surface microstructure of CoCrFeMnNi via mechanical processes can reduce friction in vacuum, relying on the formation of an ultra-fine tribolayer. More recently (PMC8470387, 2021), studies replaced or supplemented CoCrFeNi with W-rich phases to improve wear resistance above 800 °C. While these approaches demonstrated some success in targeted temperature ranges, a straightforward and single-step strategy to maintain low friction and wear from room temperature up to 800 °C in an ambient environment remains elusive, especially without recourse to further alloying additions.
decision.unsolved: A single-step method to achieve a stable, low friction coefficient and wear rate in CoCrFeNi from ~25 °C to ~800 °C—without relying on composition changes—has yet to be reliably demonstrated. The challenge is to utilize the intrinsic chemistry of CoCrFeNi while controlling surface reactions or microstructure evolution so that protective tribofilms form and remain stable over the entire temperature range in air.
decision.lever: Pre-oxidation treatment to create a stable chromium-rich oxide tribofilm on the CoCrFeNi surface; e.g. a short, controlled exposure (10–30 min) at ~700 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere to grow an adherent protective scale that remains stable across 25–800 °C sliding.
decision.why: Prior results (especially from PMC7311485) confirm that protective surface layers can drastically reduce friction and wear of CoCrFeNi-based alloys, while PMC8470387 highlights the critical role of robust oxide or intermetallic scales at high temperatures. By leveraging the alloy’s existing Cr content and deliberately forming a thin, adherent oxide before high-temperature operation, one can enable a self-lubricating, damage-tolerant surface. Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi baseline, the controlled oxide scale should reduce direct metal–metal contact and oxidative damage, thus improving tribological performance across the full temperature range. A falsification experiment would involve repeating sliding tests on both pre-oxidized and non-oxidized reference samples under identical load (e.g., 10 N) at incremental temperatures from 25 °C to 800 °C in air. If the oxide scale is indeed responsible for improved tribological behavior, removing or disrupting it (e.g., by mechanical polishing) should yield friction and wear rates similar to the untreated baseline.
